read.sections.0.text.source: The Banda Islands are small islands in eastern Indonesia. For hundreds of years, they were the only place in the world where nutmeg trees grew. The tree's seed gives nutmeg, and the red skin around the seed gives a spice called mace. Buyers far away paid a lot for both. Traders came from Indonesia, China, India, Persia and Arabia. Later, ships came from Portugal, the Netherlands and England. Bandanese leaders were skilled traders, and they chose whom to sell to. Selling spice also paid for food, because the islands grew very little.
read.sections.0.text.note: nutmeg = ลูกจันทน์เทศ (glossary word) and mace = ดอกจันทน์ (the usual Thai name for the aril; รกจันทน์ is also used). Banda Islands = หมู่เกาะบันดา, Banda Neira = บันดาเนรา, Banda Besar = บันดาเบซาร์ (Latin in brackets in the evidence once). Check the spellings.
read.sections.0.text.back: The Banda Islands are small islands in eastern Indonesia. For hundreds of years this was the only place in the world where nutmeg trees grew. The tree's seed gives nutmeg, and the red covering around the seed gives a spice called mace. Faraway buyers were willing to pay a lot for both. Traders came from Indonesia, China, India, Persia and Arabia, and later ships came from Portugal, the Netherlands and England. Bandanese leaders were skilled traders and chose for themselves whom to sell to. Selling spices also gave them money to buy food, because very few crops could be grown on the islands.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: The Banda Islands are in Indonesia. For a long time, only Banda had nutmeg trees. Nutmeg is a spice from the seed. Mace is a spice from the red skin on the seed. People far away paid a lot for them. Traders came from many places in Asia, and later from Europe. Banda's leaders were good traders. They chose who to sell to.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: The Banda Islands are in Indonesia. For a long time, only Banda had nutmeg trees. Nutmeg is a spice from the seed. Mace is a spice from the red covering around the seed. People far away paid a lot to buy them. Traders came from many places in Asia, and later from Europe. Banda's leaders were good at trade. They chose for themselves whom to sell to.

read.sections.1.text.source: The Dutch East India Company, called the VOC, wanted a monopoly. It wanted to be the only buyer of Banda's nutmeg, so no one else could compete. In 1609, a VOC fleet came to Banda Neira, one of the islands, and began to build a fort. The people there refused the company's demands, and years of fighting followed. In 1621, a VOC force led by Jan Pieterszoon Coen attacked the islands. Many Bandanese people were killed. Others were enslaved or forced to leave. Some escaped to other islands, where people kept Banda's history alive in songs and dances. After 1621, the VOC gave the land to settlers, and enslaved people were forced to grow the nutmeg.
read.sections.1.text.note: VOC = บริษัทอินเดียตะวันออกของดัตช์ the first time, then VOC (KEY_TERMS). monopoly = การผูกขาด. Coen's name is written ยัน ปีเตอร์ซูน โกน in the reading (read aloud) and Jan Pieterszoon Coen in the evidence; Thai books also write ยาน ปีเตอร์สซูน โคน. Check the usual Thai form.
read.sections.1.text.back: The Dutch East India Company, called the VOC, wanted a monopoly. It wanted to be the only buyer of Banda's nutmeg, so that no one could compete. In 1609, a VOC fleet reached Banda Neira, one island in the group, and began building a fort. People there refused the company's demands, and there were years of fighting. In 1621, VOC forces led by Jan Pieterszoon Coen attacked the islands. Many Bandanese people were killed. Some were enslaved or forced to leave. Some fled to other islands, where people kept Banda's history alive in songs and dances. After 1621, the VOC gave land to settlers, and enslaved people were forced to grow nutmeg.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: A Dutch company called the VOC came to Banda. It wanted a monopoly. It wanted to be the only buyer of nutmeg. In 1609, it began to build a fort. The people of Banda said no. They fought for years. In 1621, the VOC attacked again. Many Bandanese people were killed. Others were made slaves or forced to leave. Some escaped to other islands. They kept Banda's history alive in songs and dances. Then enslaved people had to grow the nutmeg.
read.sections.1.simpler.note: 'enslaved' = ถูกจับเป็นทาส in the simpler text, ถูกทำให้เป็นทาส in the standard text (closer to 'enslaved' than เป็นทาส, which can sound like a status they had).
read.sections.1.simpler.back: A Dutch company called the VOC came to Banda. The company wanted a monopoly. It wanted to be the only buyer of nutmeg. In 1609, the company began building a fort. The Bandanese did not agree. They fought for years. In 1621, the VOC attacked again. Many Bandanese people were killed. Some were taken as slaves or forced to leave. Some fled to other islands. They kept Banda's history in songs and dances. Then enslaved people had to grow nutmeg.

read.sections.2.text.source: The second picture is a painting of Banda Neira from about 1662, more than 40 years after the attack. The VOC paid a painters' workshop in the Netherlands to make it. It shows forts, a ship, houses and neat rows of nutmeg trees. It does not show the people who were harmed, or the people who worked in those gardens. The painting shows the company's perspective. Coen's own reports from 1621 are company sources too. In his letters, he wrote that almost nobody escaped, but that was not true. So historians compare sources, and they also listen to the songs and stories that Bandanese people passed down.
read.sections.2.text.back: The second picture is a painting of Banda Neira from about 1662, more than 40 years after the attack. The VOC hired a painters' workshop in the Netherlands to paint it. It shows a fort, ships, houses and nutmeg trees planted in neat rows. It does not show people who were harmed, or people working in those plantations. This painting shows the company's point of view. Coen's own report from 1621 is also a company source. In his letters he wrote that almost no one escaped, but that is not true. So historians compare sources, and also listen to the songs and stories the Bandanese passed down.

read.sections.2.simpler.source: The second picture is a painting. It was made about 40 years after the attack. The VOC paid for it. It shows a fort, a ship and nutmeg trees. It does not show the people who were hurt. It shows the company's perspective. Coen wrote reports too. He said almost nobody escaped. That was not true. So historians check many sources. They also listen to Bandanese songs and stories.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: The second picture is a painting. It was painted about 40 years after the attack. The VOC paid for it. It shows a fort, ships and nutmeg trees. It does not show people who were harmed. This picture shows the company's point of view. Coen also wrote a report. He said almost no one escaped, which is not true. So historians check many sources, and also listen to the songs and stories of the Bandanese.

sensitiveNotes.0.source: This lesson covers the VOC's conquest of Banda in 1621: mass killing, enslavement and forced removal. The Dutch National Archives' teaching page is titled “Genocide op Banda (1621)”. Learner text states it plainly, once, with no detail and no death toll; sources give different numbers (the archives: up to 15,000 people before, about 1,000 left on the islands; the Rijksmuseum: all 15,000 killed or driven away), so never ask learners to learn a figure. Some learners may have lived through violence or forced displacement: say before part 2 what it covers, let anyone read the simpler text or step away, and never ask learners about their own or their family's experiences of war, displacement, their country, religion or ethnicity. Don't present the events as a disagreement with two equal sides, and never invent a Bandanese first-person quotation. The TED-Ed video in the sources (Adam Clulow) describes the violence in far more detail than the lesson: watch it yourself before showing any of it.
sensitiveNotes.0.note: 'Genocide op Banda' glossed as การฆ่าล้างเผ่าพันธุ์ที่บันดา, the standard Thai word for genocide. Keep it in the teachers' note only, as the English does. Second pass: the last English sentence (the TED-Ed video describes the violence in far more detail; preview it first) was missing and has been added. Note for the team: the English sentence says 'see its note', but SAT04 has no Watch step (watch is null); the TED-Ed talk is only in the sources. Check the English.
sensitiveNotes.0.back: This lesson talks about the VOC's conquest of Banda in 1621, which involved mass killing, enslavement and forced removal. The Dutch National Archives' teaching page is titled "Genocide op Banda (1621)" (Genocide on Banda, 1621). The learner text states this directly once, without detail and without death tolls. Sources give different numbers (the Archives: up to 15,000 people before, about 1,000 left on the islands; the Rijksmuseum: all 15,000 killed or driven out), so don't have learners memorise numbers. Some learners may have experienced violence or forced displacement. Say before part 2 what it covers, let anyone read the simpler version or take a break, and do not ask learners about their own or their family's experiences of war, displacement, country, religion or ethnicity. Don't present the events as a debate with two equal sides, and don't invent words for Bandanese people. The TED-Ed video in the list of sources (Adam Clulow) describes the violence in much more detail than the lesson. Watch it yourself before letting learners see any part of it.

educatorNotes.0.source: Aim: learners name the VOC's monopoly and the harm it brought, and say whose account a company source leaves out. Evidence move (brief 3B): read Coen's report as a company source (he led the attack, and the archives show his claim that almost nobody escaped was false: about 1,700 Bandanese escaped), then look at the later commissioned painting. A sound answer names the monopoly and the harm and identifies a missing account. Misconception to catch: a fort or an orderly ship in the painting does not prove trade was voluntary or that the VOC caused no harm. Banda's history did not end in 1621: people who escaped kept it alive, for example in the Kei Islands, through songs and dances such as the Wanar dance (Dutch National Archives).
educatorNotes.0.back: Goal: learners can say what the VOC's monopoly was and what harm it brought, and say whose stories the company's sources are missing. Evidence skill (brief 3B): read Coen's report as a company source (he led the attack, and the Archives show his claim that almost no one escaped was false; about 1,700 Bandanese escaped), then look at the painting the company commissioned later. A good answer names the monopoly and the harm, and names a missing story. Misconception to watch for: a neat-looking fort or ships in the painting do not prove that trade was voluntary or that the VOC harmed no one. Banda's history did not end in 1621. People who escaped kept this history alive, for example in the Kei Islands, through songs and dances such as the Wanar dance (Dutch National Archives).

educatorNotes.1.source: Source caveats: the Dutch National Archives says its collection holds no sources with Bandanese voices, so every archive source on Banda tells the story from a colonial view. Its page shows Coen's 6 May 1621 report on the decision to starve out Banda Besar; the lesson describes it only in general terms and never quotes it. The Rijksmuseum says the painting was commissioned by the VOC's Amsterdam chamber from the Vingboons workshop before 30 April 1663, probably for the directors' meeting room, and was based on company maps: Neira never had five nutmeg gardens, and the hills behind are imagined. Before the VOC, the Westfries Museum says Dutch traders at first paid port fees and bought spice like other visitors, which helps show the change from trade to force.
